messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 51-year-old widowed school principal who came to treatment after months of trying to organize himself around a fear he could not neatly explain to other people. The traumatic event was a life-threatening illness that unfolded in the clinical world he now goes to considerable lengths to avoid. He described stretches of that period as strangely inaccessible when he tries to call them up on purpose, as if the worst parts will not line up into a coherent story when he reaches for them directly. What remains sharply present are sensory fragments and bodily states. He remembers the smell of antiseptic in treatment rooms and, at other moments, the sour, medicinal smell of alcohol swabs and hand sanitizer just before someone touched him or prepared a procedure. During examinations he had lain still in a rigid, exposed position, acutely aware that his survival depended on other people and on a body that no longer felt dependable. What frightened him most was not just the possibility of dying, but the realization that his own body could turn dangerous and incomprehensible to him.

In the months after he recovered enough to return to work, David expected to feel grateful and resume his old life. Instead he found that ordinary moments at school could abruptly take on the force of the hospital. A custodian cleaning a hallway with a sharp disinfectant, a nurse opening an alcohol wipe in the front office, even stepping into the school health room could stop him cold. At those times he did not necessarily see a full picture in his mind. More often the feeling arrived first and all at once, with the same intensity he had felt when he was critically ill. He would go tense and still, and he noticed his body seeming to brace into the same position he had been in during examinations, as if he were back on a table waiting for something to be done to him. Because the memories were so difficult to retrieve deliberately, these moments felt even more unsettling to him; he could not tell himself a complete story and set it aside. He was left with the conviction that his body knew something catastrophic before his mind could catch up.

David had once thought of himself as composed, socially capable, and dependable under pressure, qualities that had served him well as a principal. Since the illness, he has come to feel that “the person I’ve become” is someone he barely recognizes. He no longer trusts his body, reading normal sensations with suspicion and feeling that it could fail him again without warning. Alongside that is a quieter but equally painful belief that he cannot rely on himself. In meetings with teachers or parents, he now rehearses conversations in advance, sometimes word for word, before any interaction. He does not describe this as perfectionism so much as self-protection: if he scripts what he will say, perhaps he will not falter, freeze, or reveal how unsettled he feels. Even brief unscheduled conversations in the hallway can leave him internally scrambling.

Outside work his world has narrowed. Widowed before the illness, David had already been accustomed to managing much of life alone, but over time he cut off nearly all contact with friends and extended family. Texts go unanswered, invitations are declined, and phone calls are allowed to ring out. He says it feels easier not to explain himself, easier not to be seen as altered or fragile. The isolation has had visible consequences. Colleagues have noticed he no longer joins staff dinners or community events, and a sister who used to speak with him weekly now hears from him only sporadically. At school he avoids situations that might bring him close to medical cues. He delegates student hospital visits to assistant administrators, takes routes that bypass the nurse’s office, and has put off his own physical examinations despite knowing they are important. The idea of sitting in an exam room, smelling antiseptic, waiting for a clinician to begin, feels intolerable.

What finally brought David in was a recent medical appointment he had delayed and then forced himself to attend. As soon as he entered the clinic and caught the smell of alcohol and disinfectant, the emotional force hit before any clear image did. His body tightened into that familiar frozen posture, and afterward he sat in his car unable to drive for several minutes, shaken and ashamed. That episode frightened him not only because it was intense, but because it confirmed how little command he feels he has over himself and over his body. By the time he sought help, he was living with the sense that his life had become organized around avoiding reminders and concealing how changed he feels. What he fears most is that he will never again be able to trust his body or recognize himself in the person he has become. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to enter a medical office or walk past the school nurse’s door without feeling as though he is back in the worst moments of his illness.
